claim: Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers and the second leading cause of cancer-related death for men in western countries.
source: Prostate cancer (PCa) is one of the most common cancers and the second leading cause of cancer-related death for men in western countries (Siegel et al., 2022; Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Siegel et al., 2022 and Sung et al., 2021

claim: Advanced prostate cancer initially responds to androgen deprivation therapy but invariably fails and recurs as lethal castration-resistant prostate cancer.
source: Advanced PCa initially responds to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), but invariably fails and recurs as lethal castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) (Harris et al., 2009; Desai et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris et al., 2009 and Desai et al., 2021

claim: Androgen receptor signaling plays a crucial role in the progress and survival of CRPC.
source: Androgen receptor (AR) signaling plays a crucial role in the progress and survival of CRPC (Dai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dai et al., 2017

claim: Second-generation antiandrogens improve overall survival time and decline prostate-specific antigen levels in patients with CRPC.
source: Second-generation antiandrogens (SGAs), such as enzalutamide (ENZa), abiraterone, apalutamide, and darolutamide, improve the overall survival time and decline prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels in patients with CRPC (Sternberg et al., 2020; Armstrong et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2022; Ryan et al., 2015; de Bono et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to clinical studies

claim: The success of second-generation antiandrogens in treating CRPC has been eliminated by the emergence of drug resistance.
source: Despite the initial benefit of these agents, their success in treating CRPC has been eliminated by the emergence of drug resistance.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the manuscript

claim: Multiple mechanisms for the development of drug resistance include mutations in the AR LBD, amplification of AR, expression of AR splice variants, and intra-tumoral de novo androgen synthesis.
source: Multiple possible mechanisms for the development of drug resistance have thus far been identified, including mutations in the AR LBD, amplification of AR, expression of AR splice variants (ARVs), and intra-tumoral de novo androgen synthesis (Buttigliero et al., 2015; Robinson et al., 2015; Karantanos et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buttigliero et al., 2015; Robinson et al., 2015; Karantanos et al., 2015

claim: Approximately 7.5 million compounds were screened from the ZINC lead-like database and ChemDiv database.
source: we previously constructed a common molecular characteristic pharmacophore model, and screened ~7.5 million compounds from the ZINC lead-like database and ChemDiv database.
evidence: Described as a method performed by the authors

claim: About 47,202 compounds matched more than four features of the filtering model.
source: About 47,202 compounds matched more than four features of the filtering model.
evidence: Reported as a result from the screening process

claim: 80 hits with high drug-likeness were selected and purchased for further bioactivity evaluation.
source: Finally, 80 hits with high drug-likeness were selected and purchased for further bioactivity evaluation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Reported as a result from the screening process and referenced in supplementary figure

claim: 19 compounds showed more than 25% AR transcription inhibition activity.
source: We identified 19 compounds that showed more than 25% AR transcription inhibition activity, among which compound Z15 (structure shown in Figure 1A) exhibited the most potent AR inhibition activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Reported as experimental result with reference to figure

claim: Compound Z15 exhibited the most potent AR inhibition activity among the 19 compounds tested.
source: We identified 19 compounds that showed more than 25% AR transcription inhibition activity, among which compound Z15 (structure shown in Figure 1A) exhibited the most potent AR inhibition activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).

claim: The glucocorticoid receptor transcription inhibition activity of Z15 was quite feeble.

claim: Z15 could inhibit DHT-induced transcriptional activities of both exogenous and endogenous AR in a dose-dependent manner.

claim: Z15 showed potent AR transcription inhibition activity in AR overexpression and ENZa-insensitive VCaP cells.

claim: Z15 is a highly selective AR inhibitor.

The results revealed that Z15 significantly inhibited the mRNA expression levels of these genes (Figure 2B), consistent with the findings of RNA-sequencing.
